P.title: P.blurb
History: The turning points of humanity, from the first farmers to the digital age.

P.title: hi-turns.summary
History: Five changes that made the modern world, in the order they happened.

P.title: hi-turns.q0.q
History: What was most early writing used for?

P.title: hi-turns.q0.o1
History: Keeping accounts of goods and payments

P.title: hi-turns.q0.x
History: The earliest Sumerian tablets are mostly records of grain, livestock and rations.

P.title: hi-turns.q1.q
History: Why did farming lead to cities?

P.title: hi-turns.q1.o1
History: Food surpluses could feed people who didn't farm

P.title: hi-turns.q1.o2
History: Cities were needed to store tools

P.title: hi-turns.q1.x
History: Surplus food supported specialists, rulers and traders, which made towns and cities possible.

P.title: hi-turns.q2.q
History: Where and when did Gutenberg's press appear?

P.title: hi-turns.q2.x
History: Gutenberg worked in Mainz around 1450. (Movable type existed earlier in China and Korea, but his press transformed Europe.)

P.title: hi-turns.q3.q
History: Where did Homo sapiens first evolve?

P.title: hi-turns.q3.x
History: Modern humans spread out from Africa.

P.title: hi-turns.q4.q
History: Where were the first coins minted?

P.title: hi-turns.c0.text
History: Squeeze the roughly 300,000 years of Homo sapiens into a single day. For almost all of it, everyone lived as hunter-gatherers.\n\nFarming only starts at about 23:02. Writing appears at 23:36. The printing press arrives less than three minutes before midnight, and everything since the steam engine fits in the last minute.

P.title: hi-turns.c0.sketch.13
History: zoom: the last hour of the day

P.title: hi-turns.c1.text
History: Around 10,000 BCE, people in the Fertile Crescent (today's Iraq, Syria and Turkey) began planting wheat and barley and keeping animals.\n\nFarming made food surpluses possible. Surpluses could be stored, traded and taxed, and they fed people who didn't farm: potters, priests, soldiers and kings. Villages grew into the first cities.

P.title: hi-turns.c2.text
History: The oldest writing we know comes from Sumer, in today's Iraq, around 3200 BCE. It wasn't poetry. It was accounts: who delivered how much barley, how many sheep, how much beer was paid as wages.\n\nScribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay with a reed. We call the script cuneiform, from the Latin for 'wedge'.

P.title: hi-turns.c3.text
History: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine making. A book that took a scribe months could now be printed by the hundred.\n\nWithin 50 years millions of books were in circulation. Ideas spread faster than authorities could control them, feeding the Reformation and the scientific revolution.

P.title: hi-turns.c4.text
History: From about 1760 in Britain, machines powered by water and then coal-fired steam engines took over spinning, weaving and mining. Work moved from homes and fields into factories, and people moved into fast-growing cities.\n\nFor the first time in history, output per person kept rising decade after decade. It also brought child labour, pollution and the start of large-scale CO₂ emissions.

P.title: hi-turns.c5.text
History: Long before farming, humans controlled fire, cooked food and made ever better stone tools. Cooking made food easier to digest and may have helped our ancestors grow bigger brains.

P.title: hi-turns.c6.text
History: Modern humans evolved in Africa and spread across the world in waves, reaching Europe around 45,000 years ago, Australia perhaps 50,000–65,000 years ago and the Americas at least 15,000 years ago.

P.title: hi-turns.c7.text
History: With farming came the first cities in Mesopotamia, such as Uruk and Ur, around 4000–3000 BCE: temples, kings, laws, taxes and soldiers.

P.title: hi-turns.c8.text
History: Before coins, people traded goods or used standard weights of silver and grain. The first coins appeared in Lydia (modern Turkey) around 600 BCE. China later invented paper money.

P.title: hi-turns.c9.text
History: The latest turning point: computers, the internet and smartphones connected most of humanity within a few decades and changed how we work, learn and communicate.

P.title: hi-egypt.summary
History: Pyramids, pharaohs and the gift of the Nile.

P.title: hi-egypt.q0.q
History: Why did Egyptian farming depend on the Nile?

P.title: hi-egypt.q0.o1
History: Its yearly flood left fertile silt

P.title: hi-egypt.c0.text
History: Egypt's civilisation grew along the Nile. Each year the river flooded and left fertile black silt, letting farmers grow wheat and barley in the middle of the desert.

P.title: hi-egypt.c1.text
History: Egyptian history spans about 3,000 years, usually divided into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of disunity.

P.title: hi-egypt.c2.text
History: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE, with about 2.3 million stone blocks. It was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

P.title: hi-egypt.c3.text
History: Not slaves, as often claimed, but organised teams of paid workers and farmers working during the flood season, housed in villages nearby. Their tombs and bakeries have been excavated.

P.title: hi-egypt.c3.viz.items.0.r
History: built by organised, paid labour teams

P.title: hi-egypt.c4.text
History: Egyptians wrote with hieroglyphs: pictures standing for sounds and ideas. The Rosetta Stone, carrying the same text in three scripts, let Champollion decode them in 1822.

P.title: hi-egypt.c4.viz.steps.1
History: Same text in Greek and Egyptian scripts

P.title: hi-egypt.c5.text
History: Egyptians believed the body was needed in the afterlife. Embalmers removed organs, dried the body with natron salt for about 40 days and wrapped it in linen.

P.title: hi-egypt.c6.text
History: The pharaoh was seen as a living god and link between people and the divine. Egyptians worshipped many gods: Ra the sun, Osiris of the afterlife, Isis, Horus and Anubis.

P.title: hi-egypt.c7.text
History: A minor boy-king who died around 19, Tutankhamun became famous because his tomb was found almost intact by Howard Carter in 1922, full of treasures including the golden mask.

P.title: hi-egypt.c8.text
History: Egyptians developed a 365-day calendar, practical geometry for re-measuring fields after floods, medicine recorded on papyrus and remarkable engineering.

P.title: hi-egypt.c9.text
History: Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom, was of Macedonian Greek descent. After her defeat with Mark Antony, Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE.

P.title: hi-greece.q0.q
History: Who could vote in Athenian democracy?

P.title: hi-greece.q2.q
History: When were the modern Olympics revived?

P.title: hi-greece.q2.x
History: Pierre de Coubertin led the revival.

P.title: hi-greece.c0.text
History: Ancient Greece wasn't one country but hundreds of city-states (poleis) like Athens, Sparta, Corinth and Thebes, sharing a language and gods but often at war with each other.

P.title: hi-greece.c1.text
History: From around 508 BCE, Athenian citizens voted directly on laws in the Assembly. But only free adult men counted as citizens: women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.

P.title: hi-greece.c2.text
History: Greek thinkers asked how we should live and how the world works. Socrates questioned everything, Plato founded the Academy, Aristotle studied everything from logic to biology.

P.title: hi-greece.c3.text
History: Persia's huge empire invaded Greece twice. The Greeks won at Marathon (490 BCE), held the pass at Thermopylae long enough, and won the naval battle of Salamis (480 BCE).

P.title: hi-greece.c4.text
History: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia every four years from 776 BCE, in honour of Zeus. Wars paused for the games. The modern Olympics were revived in Athens in 1896.

P.title: hi-greece.c5.text
History: Alexander of Macedon conquered an empire from Greece to Egypt and India before dying at 32 in 323 BCE. Greek language and culture spread across the region (the Hellenistic age).

P.title: hi-greece.c6.text
History: Euclid's geometry, Archimedes' physics, Hippocrates' medicine and Eratosthenes' measurement of Earth's circumference all came from the Greek world.

P.title: hi-greece.c7.text
History: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared the Sun's angle at noon in Syene and Alexandria. From a 7° difference and the distance between the cities, he estimated Earth's circumference remarkably well.

P.title: hi-greece.c8.text
History: Greeks invented tragedy and comedy as theatre forms. Huge open-air theatres like Epidaurus have such good acoustics that a whisper on stage can be heard in the back rows.

P.title: hi-greece.c9.text
History: Many English and Portuguese words come from Greek: democracy, philosophy, theatre, telephone, biology, geography, mathematics.

P.title: hi-china.summary
History: Dynasties, inventions and exams across more than 3,000 years.

P.title: hi-china.q0.x
History: He took the new title "First Emperor".

P.title: hi-china.q1.q
History: What were Shang oracle bones used for?

P.title: hi-china.q1.x
History: Diviners heated them and read the cracks.

P.title: hi-china.q2.q
History: Which dynasty built most of the stone and brick Great Wall seen today?

P.title: hi-china.q3.q
History: Which is NOT one of China's four great inventions?

P.title: hi-china.q3.x
History: The four are paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder.

P.title: hi-china.q4.q
History: When did the last emperor, Puyi, abdicate?

P.title: hi-china.q4.x
History: The Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 January 1912.

P.title: hi-china.c0.text
History: China's oldest writing survives on bones. Around 1200 BCE, kings of the Shang dynasty asked their ancestors about harvests, wars and illness by heating ox shoulder blades and turtle shells until they cracked.\n\nDiviners read the cracks and carved the question, and sometimes the result, into the bone. Those signs are the direct ancestors of today's Chinese characters.

P.title: hi-china.c1.text
History: After centuries of war between rival states, King Zheng of Qin conquered them all and in 221 BCE declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the "First Emperor".\n\nHe ruled through appointed officials rather than nobles, and imposed one script, one currency and one system of weights. His dynasty collapsed soon after his death, but the idea of a single China lasted.

P.title: hi-china.c2.text
History: The Great Wall is not one wall but many, built over about 2,000 years by different states and dynasties to guard farmland against horsemen from the northern steppe.\n\nThe famous stone and brick sections near Beijing are fairly recent: most were built by the Ming dynasty, mainly in the 1500s. Older walls were mostly made of rammed earth.

P.title: hi-china.c3.title
History: The Han and the Silk Road

P.title: hi-china.c3.text
History: The Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) ruled about as many people as the Roman Empire, at the same time. Most Chinese people still call themselves Han.\n\nHan armies and envoys opened routes through Central Asia. Along them, silk travelled west, while horses, new crops and, later, Buddhism came east.

P.title: hi-china.c4.text
History: For about 1,300 years, from 605 to 1905, China chose many of its officials through written exams on the Confucian classics, rather than by birth alone.\n\nCandidates memorised hundreds of thousands of characters of ancient text and wrote essays on how to govern. Passing brought prestige, power and wealth to a whole family.

P.title: hi-china.c5.text
History: Paper, printing, the magnetic compass and gunpowder are often called China's "four great inventions". Each one later spread west and changed the world.\n\nIn 1620 the English philosopher Francis Bacon wrote that printing, gunpowder and the compass had transformed the world more than any empire. He did not know where they came from.

P.title: hi-china.c6.text
History: The Tang dynasty (618–907) ruled from Chang'an, perhaps the world's largest city, full of merchants, monks and envoys from across Asia. It was the golden age of Chinese poetry.\n\nThe Song (960–1279) was weaker militarily but richer: rice farming boomed, cities grew, and the government issued the world's first paper money.

P.title: hi-china.c7.text
History: Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven huge fleets across the Indian Ocean, reaching India, Arabia and East Africa.\n\nThe voyages showed off Ming power and collected tribute. Then they stopped: the court turned inward, and China left the oceans to others, decades before the Portuguese arrived.

P.title: hi-china.c8.text
History: In 1644 the Manchus, from the north-east, took Beijing and founded the Qing, China's last dynasty. Under emperors such as Kangxi and Qianlong it nearly doubled in size and grew rich.\n\nIn the 1800s it faced rising Western powers, two Opium Wars, unequal treaties and a devastating civil war, the Taiping Rebellion.

P.title: hi-china.c9.text
History: After defeats by Western powers and by Japan, reforms came too late. In October 1911 an army uprising in Wuchang spread across the provinces.\n\nOn 1 January 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed, and in February the six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicated. More than 2,000 years of imperial rule, begun by the First Emperor in 221 BCE, were over.

P.title: hi-rome.summary
History: From a small city to ruling the Mediterranean, including Lusitania.

P.title: hi-rome.q0.q
History: What was Roman Portugal largely called?

P.title: hi-rome.q2.q
History: When did the western Roman Empire end?

P.title: hi-rome.q2.x
History: The last western emperor was deposed in 476.

P.title: hi-rome.c0.text
History: By tradition Rome was founded in 753 BCE. It was ruled by kings, then became a republic governed by elected officials and the Senate, then an empire under Augustus from 27 BCE.

P.title: hi-rome.c1.text
History: At its peak around 117 CE under Trajan, the empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia and from the Rhine to North Africa, with perhaps 50–70 million people.

P.title: hi-rome.c2.text
History: Much of today's Portugal became the Roman province of Lusitania, with its capital at Emerita Augusta (Mérida). The Lusitanian leader Viriato resisted Rome fiercely until his murder in 139 BCE.

P.title: hi-rome.c3.text
History: You can still see Roman Portugal: the temple at Évora, the ruins of Conímbriga, the bridge at Chaves, and countless roads. Portuguese itself descends from Latin.

P.title: hi-rome.c4.text
History: Romans built about 80,000 km of paved roads and aqueducts carrying water by gravity over long distances, using gentle slopes and arches.

P.title: hi-rome.c5.text
History: Romans used volcanic ash in concrete that has lasted 2,000 years, even in seawater. The Pantheon's dome in Rome, finished around 125 CE, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

P.title: hi-rome.c6.text
History: Roman law, later compiled under Emperor Justinian, is the basis of civil law systems across Europe and Latin America, including Portugal's.

P.title: hi-rome.c7.text
History: Latin evolved into Portuguese, Spanish, Italian, French and Romanian. About 60% of English vocabulary also comes from Latin, directly or through French.

P.title: hi-rome.c8.text
History: The western empire weakened through civil wars, economic trouble and pressure from Germanic peoples. In 476 the last western emperor was deposed. The eastern (Byzantine) empire lasted until 1453.

P.title: hi-rome.c9.text
History: Christianity spread through the empire despite persecutions. Emperor Constantine legalised it in 313, and by 380 it became the official religion.

P.title: hi-medieval.q0.q
History: What killed perhaps a third of Europe in the 1300s?

P.title: hi-medieval.q1.q
History: Who helped Afonso Henriques take Lisbon in 1147?

P.title: hi-medieval.q2.q
History: Where did Portugal's university settle permanently in 1537?

P.title: hi-medieval.q2.x
History: It moved between Lisbon and Coimbra before settling.

P.title: hi-medieval.c0.text
History: The Middle Ages run roughly from the fall of Rome (476) to the late 1400s. The name was coined later by Renaissance thinkers who saw it as a gap between antiquity and their own time.

P.title: hi-medieval.c1.text
History: Land was the main source of wealth. Kings granted land to lords in return for military service; peasants worked the land for lords in return for protection.

P.title: hi-medieval.c2.text
History: The Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in western Europe: it owned land, ran schools and hospitals, kept learning alive in monasteries and shaped daily life.

P.title: hi-medieval.c3.text
History: Castles were fortified homes and military bases. Portugal has hundreds, many built or rebuilt during the Reconquista: Guimarães, Almourol, Óbidos, Marvão.

P.title: hi-medieval.c4.text
History: From 1096, Christian armies launched crusades to take Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Crusaders also helped Afonso Henriques conquer Lisbon in 1147 on their way east.

P.title: hi-medieval.c5.text
History: Plague swept Europe from 1347, carried by fleas on rats and spread between people. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population within a few years.

P.title: hi-medieval.c6.text
History: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher wages and more freedom. Serfdom weakened in western Europe, and new ideas took root.

P.title: hi-medieval.c7.text
History: From the 1100s, pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses let builders raise tall, light cathedrals with huge stained-glass windows. The Batalha monastery is a Portuguese masterpiece.

P.title: hi-medieval.c8.text
History: Europe's first universities appeared in Bologna (1088), Paris and Oxford. Portugal's university was founded in Lisbon in 1290 and later moved permanently to Coimbra in 1537.

P.title: hi-medieval.c9.text
History: The Middle Ages brought windmills, eyeglasses, mechanical clocks, the compass in Europe, universities and great art. The idea of "dark ages" is now seen as too simple.

P.title: hi-andalus.summary
History: Muslim Iberia and the Islamic golden age.

P.title: hi-andalus.q2.q
History: When did Portugal complete its reconquest?

P.title: hi-andalus.c0.text
History: In 711, Muslim armies from North Africa crossed into Iberia and within a few years controlled most of the peninsula, including today's Portugal. They called it al-Andalus.

P.title: hi-andalus.c0.viz.events.1.l
History: most of Iberia under Muslim rule

P.title: hi-andalus.c1.text
History: In the 10th century Córdoba was one of Europe's largest and most sophisticated cities, with paved streets, lighting, baths, libraries and the great mosque.

P.title: hi-andalus.c2.text
History: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side in al-Andalus, with Christians and Jews as protected but taxed minorities. Coexistence was real but not equality, and it varied over time.

P.title: hi-andalus.c3.text
History: From roughly the 8th to 13th centuries, scholars in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba translated and extended Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.

P.title: hi-andalus.c4.text
History: The digits 0–9 came from India, reached Europe through the Arab world and are called Hindu-Arabic numerals. The word "algorithm" comes from al-Khwarizmi's name.

P.title: hi-andalus.c5.text
History: Muslim farmers introduced or spread crops like oranges, lemons, rice, almonds and sugar cane in Iberia, along with irrigation systems such as the water wheel (nora).

P.title: hi-andalus.c6.text
History: Portuguese has hundreds of words of Arabic origin, often starting with "al-": azeite, arroz, alface, almofada, açúcar, aldeia, armazém. "Oxalá" comes from "if God wills".

P.title: hi-andalus.c7.text
History: Many Portuguese places have Arabic names: the Algarve (al-gharb, "the west"), Alcácer, Alfama, Albufeira, Fátima (a Muslim name).

P.title: hi-andalus.c8.text
History: Christian kingdoms in the north gradually pushed south over nearly 800 years. Portugal completed its reconquest with the Algarve in 1249; Spain with Granada in 1492.

P.title: hi-andalus.c9.text
History: Silves was the capital of the Algarve under Muslim rule, and Mértola's church was once a mosque. Both still show their Islamic past in walls, streets and museums.

P.title: hi-mongols.summary
History: How steppe horsemen built the largest land empire in history, and what it left behind.

P.title: hi-mongols.q0.q
History: In which year was Temüjin proclaimed Genghis Khan?

P.title: hi-mongols.q0.x
History: A great assembly, the kurultai, gave him the title.

P.title: hi-mongols.q1.x
History: Riders changed horses at stations across the empire.

P.title: hi-mongols.q2.q
History: Which city did Kublai Khan build as his capital?

P.title: hi-mongols.q2.x
History: Beijing has been China's capital for most of the time since.

P.title: hi-mongols.q3.q
History: Where did the Black Death probably begin?

P.title: hi-mongols.q3.x
History: DNA from 1338–39 graves in Kyrgyzstan points there.

P.title: hi-mongols.c0.text
History: Temüjin was born around 1162 on the Mongolian steppe. After his father was poisoned, his family was abandoned and lived in poverty, hunting marmots and gathering roots.\n\nThrough alliances, loyalty and war he united the feuding steppe tribes. In 1206 a great assembly proclaimed him Genghis Khan, ruler of all the "people of the felt tents".

P.title: hi-mongols.c1.text
History: The Mongol army was made of mounted archers. Each rider carried a powerful composite bow and could shoot accurately at a gallop, standing in the stirrups.\n\nEach warrior had several horses and changed mounts to keep them fresh. Fast, disciplined units could encircle an enemy, retreat on purpose to draw it into a trap, and wheel round again.

P.title: hi-mongols.c1.viz.items.0
History: Composite bow of horn and wood

P.title: hi-mongols.c2.text
History: Mongol armies carried little and lived off their animals and the land. Riders had dried milk curd, dried meat and fermented mare's milk, and herds travelled with them.\n\nWithout slow supply wagons they could move much faster than their enemies, cross deserts and mountains, and appear where nobody expected them.

P.title: hi-mongols.c3.text
History: At its peak, around 1270, the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to Hungary and from Siberia to the Persian Gulf, about 24 million km².\n\nIt is the largest continuous land empire in history. Only the British Empire, spread across oceans, was larger in total. Yet the Mongols themselves may have numbered only about a million people.

P.title: hi-mongols.c4.text
History: To rule such distances, the Mongols built the yam, a network of relay stations across the empire, with fresh horses, food and lodging for official riders.\n\nMessengers carrying a metal tablet called a paiza could change horses at each station and ride on day and night, carrying news far faster than ever before.

P.title: hi-mongols.c5.text
History: Once the conquests settled, the Mongols ruled most of the Silk Road routes themselves. For about a century, roughly 1250 to 1350, merchants and travellers could cross Eurasia under one political umbrella.\n\nHistorians call this the Pax Mongolica, the "Mongol peace". Goods, ideas, technologies and people moved between China, Persia and Europe as never before.

P.title: hi-mongols.c6.text
History: Kublai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became Great Khan in 1260 and founded the Yuan dynasty in China in 1271. By 1279 he had conquered the Song, the first non-Chinese ruler of all China.\n\nHis capital, Dadu, grew into today's Beijing. He ruled through a mix of Mongol, Central Asian and Chinese officials and used paper money across the empire.

P.title: hi-mongols.c7.text
History: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo travelled to Kublai Khan's court with his father and uncle, stayed about 17 years and returned to Venice in 1295.\n\nLater, as a prisoner of war in Genoa, he dictated his story to a writer of romances. *The Description of the World* amazed Europe with tales of paper money, huge cities and stones that burned.

P.title: hi-mongols.c8.text
History: The Black Death probably began in Central Asia in the 1330s. The same Mongol-era trade routes that carried silk and spices helped carry the plague bacterium west.\n\nBy 1346 it had reached the Black Sea, where Italian merchants traded with the Mongol Golden Horde. Their ships then brought it to the Mediterranean.

P.title: hi-mongols.c9.text
History: After 1260 the empire split into four khanates ruled by different branches of Genghis Khan's family, often at war with each other.\n\nThey gradually broke up or were absorbed, but the Mongols left a deep mark: on Russia, China and Iran, on trade between East and West, and on the very idea of a world connected from end to end.

P.title: hi-americas.summary
History: Three great civilisations of the Americas, their cities, science and crops, and the conquest that ended their independence.

P.title: hi-americas.q0.q
History: Which civilisation invented a Long Count calendar with a zero?

P.title: hi-americas.q0.x
History: Their dates counted days from 3114 BCE.

P.title: hi-americas.q1.o1
History: Farm plots built up in a lake

P.title: hi-americas.q2.q
History: What did the Inca use quipus for?

P.title: hi-americas.q2.x
History: Knots in set positions stood for numbers.

P.title: hi-americas.q3.q
History: Which factor killed most indigenous people after the conquest?

P.title: hi-americas.q3.x
History: They had no immunity to Old World diseases.

P.title: hi-americas.c0.text
History: The civilisations of the Americas grew from crops domesticated there thousands of years earlier. Maize came from a wild grass in Mexico; potatoes from the high Andes.\n\nThese plants fed cities, armies and priests, just as wheat and rice did in Eurasia. Today maize and potatoes are among the most important foods on Earth.

P.title: hi-americas.c1.text
History: The Maya built hundreds of cities in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras, with stepped pyramids, palaces, plazas and ball courts.\n\nThey were never one empire. Rival city-states such as Tikal and Calakmul, each ruled by a divine king, fought and allied with each other for centuries.

P.title: hi-americas.c2.text
History: The Maya developed the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, with signs for whole words and signs for syllables.\n\nThey carved it on stone monuments, painted it on pottery and wrote books on bark paper. After years of work, scholars can now read most surviving texts: they record kings, wars, births and rituals.

P.title: hi-americas.c3.text
History: Maya numbers used just three signs: a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero. They counted in twenties, not tens.\n\nWith them they kept several calendars, including the Long Count, which numbered days from a starting point in 3114 BCE. It needed a true zero, which the Maya invented independently of India.

P.title: hi-americas.c4.text
History: The Mexica, better known as the Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. By 1519 it may have had over 200,000 people, larger than any city in Spain.\n\nIt was fed by chinampas: narrow fields built up from lake mud, separated by canals. They could give several harvests a year.

P.title: hi-americas.c5.text
History: The Inca Empire, ruled from Cusco, was the largest in the Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile. A road network of about 30,000 km held it together.\n\nThe Inca had no wheeled transport and no horses. Roads carried people on foot, llama caravans and relay runners who passed messages from station to station.

P.title: hi-americas.c6.text
History: The Inca had no writing in the usual sense. Officials kept records with quipus: bundles of coloured strings tied with knots.\n\nThe position and type of each knot stood for a number, in a base-ten system. Quipus recorded censuses, taxes and storehouse contents across the empire. Whether some also recorded words is still debated.

P.title: hi-americas.c7.text
History: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, on a ridge high above the Urubamba river in Peru.\n\nThe Spanish never found it. It became world famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham visited in 1911, guided by local farmers who already knew it well.

P.title: hi-americas.c8.text
History: Small Spanish forces conquered the Aztec and Inca empires within a few years: Hernán Cortés took Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532.\n\nSteel, horses and guns helped, but two things mattered more: thousands of indigenous allies who hated Aztec or Inca rule, and new diseases such as smallpox, which killed vast numbers.

P.title: hi-americas.c9.text
History: The empires fell, but their peoples did not vanish. Millions still speak Quechua, Maya languages and Nahuatl, and indigenous traditions shape life from Mexico to Bolivia.\n\nThe rest of the world inherited their crops, from maize, potatoes and tomatoes to chillies, cacao and vanilla, and words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and llama.

P.title: hi-renaissance.summary
History: Rebirth of art, science and ideas.

P.title: hi-renaissance.q0.q
History: Which family famously sponsored Renaissance artists in Florence?

P.title: hi-renaissance.q1.o1
History: Portugal's ornate late-Gothic architecture with maritime motifs

P.title: hi-renaissance.c0.text
History: The Renaissance ("rebirth") began in Italy in the 1300s–1400s. Scholars rediscovered Greek and Roman texts, artists studied nature and the human body, and individuals were celebrated.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c1.text
History: Florence led the way, funded by rich families like the Medici who sponsored artists, architects and scholars. Wealth from banking and trade paid for the art.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c2.text
History: Artists like Brunelleschi worked out linear perspective around 1420: parallel lines meet at a vanishing point, making flat paintings look three-dimensional.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c3.text
History: Painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, Leonardo (1452–1519) also filled notebooks with anatomy, flying machines, engineering and studies of water, a true "Renaissance man".

P.title: hi-renaissance.c4.text
History: Michelangelo (1475–1564) sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, lying on scaffolding for four years. He also designed the dome of St Peter's in Rome.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c5.text
History: Humanists believed in studying classical texts, good writing and the potential of human beings. Erasmus of Rotterdam was its most famous northern European voice.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c6.text
History: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, armillary spheres, sea creatures and coral, celebrating the voyages. The Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower are famous examples.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c7.text
History: Luís de Camões published Os Lusíadas in 1572, an epic poem about Vasco da Gama's voyage and Portuguese history, inspired by classical epics. Portugal's national day, 10 June, marks his death.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c8.text
History: Gutenberg's press (around 1450) let books and new ideas spread fast. Venice became a printing capital; the first book printed in Portugal appeared in 1487, in Hebrew, in Faro.

P.title: hi-renaissance.c9.text
History: Artists' careful observation fed into science: Vesalius' accurate anatomy (1543) and Copernicus' Sun-centred universe (1543) both appeared in the same year.

P.title: hi-reform.summary
History: New ideas about faith and nature.

P.title: hi-reform.q0.q
History: What did Luther protest against in 1517?

P.title: hi-reform.q2.q
History: What does the scientific method rely on?

P.title: hi-reform.c0.text
History: In 1517, the monk Martin Luther challenged the Church's sale of indulgences (payments to reduce punishment for sins). His protest, spread by printing, split western Christianity.

P.title: hi-reform.c0.viz.events.2.l
History: Church of England breaks with Rome

P.title: hi-reform.c1.text
History: Protestants stressed faith and the Bible read in people's own languages; the Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation, reforming itself and founding orders like the Jesuits.

P.title: hi-reform.c2.text
History: Religious division fuelled wars across Europe for over a century, culminating in the devastating Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which killed millions in central Europe.

P.title: hi-reform.c3.text
History: The Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536, persecuted New Christians (converted Jews), suspected heretics and others. Many Jewish families fled to the Netherlands, Ottoman lands and elsewhere. It was abolished in 1821.

P.title: hi-reform.c3.viz.events.0.l
History: Jews ordered to convert or leave

P.title: hi-reform.c4.text
History: In 1543 Copernicus argued that Earth and the planets orbit the Sun, not the other way round. It was a radical idea that took over a century to be widely accepted.

P.title: hi-reform.c5.text
History: Galileo's telescope observations supported Copernicus. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition forced him to recant and kept him under house arrest. The Church formally acknowledged its error in 1992.

P.title: hi-reform.c6.text
History: Thinkers like Francis Bacon and Descartes argued for learning through observation, experiment and reason rather than authority alone. This became the scientific method.

P.title: hi-reform.c7.text
History: Newton's Principia (1687) used a few laws to explain both falling objects and planetary orbits. It showed the universe follows mathematical rules, a turning point for science.

P.title: hi-reform.c8.text
History: Groups like the Royal Society in London (1660) and the French Academy of Sciences (1666) met to share experiments and published journals, the start of modern peer-reviewed science.

P.title: hi-reform.c9.text
History: Telescopes, microscopes, thermometers, barometers and pendulum clocks let scientists measure what they couldn't see before.

P.title: hi-1755.q0.q
History: When did the great Lisbon earthquake strike?

P.title: hi-1755.q1.q
History: Who led the rebuilding of Lisbon?

P.title: hi-1755.q2.q
History: Which Enlightenment writer questioned divine goodness after the disaster?

P.title: hi-1755.q2.x
History: In his poem and in Candide.

P.title: hi-1755.c0.text
History: On All Saints' Day morning, a huge earthquake struck off Portugal's coast. Churches were full and candles lit. Within minutes much of Lisbon collapsed.

P.title: hi-1755.c1.text
History: The earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5–9, was followed by a tsunami up to several metres high and by fires that burned for days. Estimates of deaths in Lisbon range from about 30,000 to 50,000 or more.

P.title: hi-1755.c2.text
History: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, later Marquis of Pombal, led the response: "bury the dead and feed the living". He organised relief, controlled prices and planned the rebuilding.

P.title: hi-1755.c3.text
History: The Baixa was rebuilt on a grid of wide straight streets with uniform buildings, using standardised parts and the earthquake-resistant gaiola pombalina.

P.title: hi-1755.c4.text
History: Pombal sent a questionnaire to every parish: when did it start, how long did it last, what damage occurred? It was one of the first systematic scientific studies of an earthquake.

P.title: hi-1755.c5.text
History: The disaster shocked Europe's thinkers. Voltaire questioned why a good God would allow it, in his "Poem on the Lisbon Disaster" and in Candide. Rousseau answered that city crowding made it worse.

P.title: hi-1755.c6.text
History: The 18th-century Enlightenment championed reason, science, religious tolerance and individual rights. Thinkers like Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire and Kant inspired revolutions.

P.title: hi-1755.c7.text
History: Pombal modernised education and trade, expelled the Jesuits (1759), created the Douro wine demarcation (1756), one of the world's first, and reduced discrimination against New Christians.

P.title: hi-1755.c8.text
History: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie (1751–1772) gathered knowledge on everything from trades to philosophy, spreading Enlightenment ideas across Europe.

P.title: hi-1755.c9.text
History: Lisbon still sits near active faults. Modern building codes, tsunami warnings and earthquake drills draw on lessons from 1755.

P.title: hi-revolutions.q0.o1
History: Portugal kept trading with Britain against his blockade

P.title: hi-revolutions.q1.q
History: Where did the Portuguese court move in 1807?

P.title: hi-revolutions.c0.text
History: Thirteen British colonies rebelled over taxation without representation. The Declaration of Independence (1776) proclaimed that all men are created equal, though slavery continued.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c1.text
History: In 1789, with France bankrupt and bread expensive, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and Parisians stormed the Bastille. Feudal privileges were abolished.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c2.text
History: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) proclaimed equality before the law, freedom of speech and the sovereignty of the nation, ideas that spread worldwide.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c3.text
History: In 1793–94, the revolutionary government executed thousands of suspected enemies by guillotine, including many revolutionaries themselves, until Robespierre himself was executed.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c4.text
History: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804 and conquered much of Europe. His Napoleonic Code influenced law across Europe, including Portugal.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c5.text
History: Because Portugal kept trading with Britain, Napoleon invaded three times from 1807. With British help under Wellington, the Portuguese resisted, including at the Lines of Torres Vedras.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c6.text
History: In 1807, as the French approached, the royal family and thousands of courtiers sailed to Brazil. Rio de Janeiro became the capital of the Portuguese empire, the only time a European capital moved to a colony.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c7.text
History: After the king returned to Portugal, his son Pedro stayed in Brazil and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor Pedro I.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c8.text
History: The 1820 revolution in Porto demanded a constitution. A civil war (1828–1834) between liberals under Pedro and absolutists under his brother Miguel ended with the liberals' victory.

P.title: hi-revolutions.c9.text
History: Inspired by the US and France, and helped by Spain's weakness under Napoleon, most of Spanish America won independence between 1810 and 1825, led by figures like Simón Bolívar.

P.title: hi-19c.summary
History: Industry, railways, empires and new ideas.

P.title: hi-19c.q0.q
History: When did Portugal's first railway open?

P.title: hi-19c.q1.q
History: What was the 1890 British Ultimatum about?

P.title: hi-19c.q1.o1
History: Portugal's plan to link Angola and Mozambique

P.title: hi-19c.q2.q
History: Which country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery?

P.title: hi-19c.c0.text
History: The first public steam railway opened in England in 1825. Railways shrank journeys from days to hours and opened markets. Portugal's first line, Lisbon to Carregado, opened in 1856.

P.title: hi-19c.c1.text
History: Steamships made ocean travel reliable, and the telegraph carried messages instantly. The first lasting transatlantic cable (1866) cut message times from weeks to minutes.

P.title: hi-19c.c1.viz.unit
History: days for a London–New York message

P.title: hi-19c.c2.text
History: Millions moved from farms to industrial cities. Conditions were harsh: long hours, child labour, crowded housing and polluted air. Reforms, unions and new laws slowly improved them.

P.title: hi-19c.c3.text
History: The 19th century produced liberalism, nationalism, socialism and Marxism, ideas about the state, nations and workers that shaped the next century.

P.title: hi-19c.c4.text
History: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833. Portugal abolished slavery in stages, completing it in 1869–1878; Brazil was the last in the Americas, in 1888.

P.title: hi-19c.c5.text
History: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers set rules for dividing Africa. By 1914, almost the whole continent was under European control.

P.title: hi-19c.c6.title
History: The Pink Map and the Ultimatum

P.title: hi-19c.c6.text
History: Portugal hoped to link Angola and Mozambique (the "Pink Map"). Britain, wanting a Cape-to-Cairo route, issued the 1890 Ultimatum, forcing Portugal to back down, a national humiliation that fuelled republicanism.

P.title: hi-19c.c7.text
History: Darwin's theory of evolution (1859), Pasteur's germ theory, vaccines, anaesthesia and antiseptic surgery transformed biology and medicine.

P.title: hi-19c.c8.text
History: Italy unified between 1859 and 1871 and Germany in 1871 under Prussia, changing Europe's balance of power and setting the stage for rivalries before 1914.

P.title: hi-19c.c9.text
History: In the last decades of the century came the telephone (1876), the light bulb (1879), electric power stations, cars (1886) and radio, the foundations of the 20th century.

P.title: hi-ww1.q0.o1
History: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

P.title: hi-ww1.q1.q
History: Where did Portuguese troops suffer heavy losses on 9 April 1918?

P.title: hi-ww1.q2.q
History: When did the armistice end the fighting?

P.title: hi-ww1.c0.text
History: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was assassinated in Sarajevo. Alliances, militarism and rivalry turned a regional crisis into a world war within weeks.

P.title: hi-ww1.c1.text
History: The Allies (France, Britain, Russia, later Italy, the USA and others including Portugal) fought the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria).

P.title: hi-ww1.c2.text
History: On the Western Front, armies dug trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. Machine guns and artillery made attacks deadly; battles like the Somme cost hundreds of thousands of lives for a few kilometres.

P.title: hi-ww1.c3.text
History: WWI introduced poison gas, tanks, warplanes, submarines and industrial-scale artillery. War had become mechanised.

P.title: hi-ww1.c4.text
History: Portugal fought in Africa to defend Angola and Mozambique, and from 1917 sent the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps to Flanders. At La Lys on 9 April 1918, Portuguese forces suffered heavy losses.

P.title: hi-ww1.c5.text
History: Whole economies served the war. Women took over factory and farm work, food was rationed and governments controlled production and news.

P.title: hi-ww1.c6.text
History: German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann telegram drew the USA into the war in 1917. Fresh American troops helped tip the balance in 1918. Russia left the war after its revolution.

P.title: hi-ww1.c7.text
History: Around 9–10 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Then the 1918 flu pandemic killed tens of millions more worldwide.

P.title: hi-ww1.c8.text
History: The 1919 peace treaty blamed Germany, imposed heavy reparations and took territory. Empires collapsed: Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and the Russian Empire. New nations appeared.

P.title: hi-ww1.c9.text
History: Resentment in Germany, economic crisis and unresolved disputes helped extremists rise, leading to another world war only 20 years later.

P.title: hi-interwar.q0.q
History: When was the Portuguese republic proclaimed?

P.title: hi-interwar.q1.o1
History: The Great Depression, with the Wall Street crash

P.title: hi-interwar.c0.text
History: After the war, the 1920s brought jazz, cinema, radio, cars and booming stock markets in the USA, along with new freedoms for women, including the vote in many countries.

P.title: hi-interwar.c1.text
History: In October 1929 the New York stock market collapsed. Banks failed, trade shrank and unemployment soared worldwide: the Great Depression.

P.title: hi-interwar.c2.text
History: After the 1917 revolution, the Bolsheviks created the Soviet Union. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation and purges killed millions, including in the Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) of 1932–33.

P.title: hi-interwar.c3.text
History: Mussolini took power in 1922 and built a one-party state with censorship, a personality cult and aggressive nationalism: fascism.

P.title: hi-interwar.c4.text
History: In Germany, the Depression helped the Nazi party grow. Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and quickly destroyed democracy, persecuted Jews and opponents, and rearmed.

P.title: hi-interwar.c5.text
History: The monarchy fell on 5 October 1910. The First Republic separated church and state and expanded education, but was unstable: 45 governments in 16 years.

P.title: hi-interwar.c6.text
History: After a military coup in 1926, finance minister António de Oliveira Salazar became prime minister in 1932 and created the Estado Novo, an authoritarian, corporatist regime with censorship and a political police (PVDE, later PIDE).

P.title: hi-interwar.c7.text
History: From 1936 to 1939, Spain's republic fought Franco's nationalists, who were helped by Germany and Italy. Franco won and ruled Spain until 1975. Portugal's regime supported Franco.

P.title: hi-interwar.c8.text
History: In the USA, Roosevelt's New Deal created public works, social security and bank regulation to fight the Depression, expanding the role of government.

P.title: hi-interwar.c9.text
History: Britain and France tried to avoid war by giving in to Hitler's demands, accepting Austria's annexation and, at Munich in 1938, part of Czechoslovakia. It failed.

P.title: hi-ww2.q0.q
History: Which Portuguese consul saved thousands of refugees in 1940?

P.title: hi-ww2.q2.q
History: What did Portugal sell to both sides during WWII?

P.title: hi-ww2.q2.x
History: A vital metal for armour and tools.

P.title: hi-ww2.c0.text
History: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war. By mid-1940, Germany had conquered much of western Europe, including France.

P.title: hi-ww2.c0.viz.events.1.l
History: Denmark, Norway, Low Countries, France fall

P.title: hi-ww2.c1.text
History: In 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union, and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing the USA into the war. Fighting spread across Europe, Africa, Asia and the oceans.

P.title: hi-ww2.c2.text
History: Nazi Germany systematically murdered about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners, political opponents and others, in ghettos, mass shootings and death camps like Auschwitz.

P.title: hi-ww2.c3.text
History: In June 1940, Portugal's consul in Bordeaux, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, defied Salazar's orders and issued thousands of visas to refugees, many of them Jews. He was punished and died poor; he's now honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.

P.title: hi-ww2.c3.viz.steps.2
History: Sousa Mendes issues thousands of visas

P.title: hi-ww2.c4.text
History: Portugal stayed officially neutral, selling tungsten (volfrâmio) to both sides. Lisbon became a hub of spies and a gateway for refugees escaping to the Americas. In 1943 it let the Allies use bases in the Azores.

P.title: hi-ww2.c4.viz.items.0
History: Neutral but pro-Allied in the end

P.title: hi-ww2.c5.text
History: On 6 June 1944, Allied forces landed in Normandy in the largest seaborne invasion in history, opening a western front as the Soviets advanced from the east.

P.title: hi-ww2.c6.text
History: Soviet troops took Berlin; Hitler killed himself; Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945 (VE Day).

P.title: hi-ww2.c7.text
History: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August), killing well over 100,000 people. Japan surrendered on 15 August, formally on 2 September.

P.title: hi-ww2.c8.text
History: World War II killed an estimated 70–85 million people, most of them civilians. The Soviet Union and China suffered the largest losses.

P.title: hi-ww2.c9.text
History: The United Nations was founded in 1945, war criminals were tried at Nuremberg, and Europe was divided between western democracies and Soviet-controlled states.

P.title: hi-coldwar.summary
History: Superpowers, nuclear fear and a divided world, 1947–1991.

P.title: hi-coldwar.q0.q
History: When did the Berlin Wall fall?

P.title: hi-coldwar.q1.q
History: Who was the first human in space?

P.title: hi-coldwar.q2.q
History: Why was dictatorship-era Portugal a NATO founding member?

P.title: hi-coldwar.q2.o1
History: The Azores base was strategically important

P.title: hi-coldwar.c0.text
History: After 1945, the USA and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers with opposing systems: capitalist democracy versus communist one-party rule. They never fought each other directly.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c1.text
History: Europe was split. Churchill spoke of an "iron curtain" in 1946. Germany was divided, and in 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing west.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c2.text
History: Both sides built tens of thousands of nuclear weapons. The doctrine of "mutually assured destruction" meant any nuclear war would destroy both.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c3.text
History: In October 1962, the USA discovered Soviet missiles in Cuba. For 13 days the world stood close to nuclear war, until the USSR agreed to withdraw them and the USA quietly removed missiles from Turkey.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c4.text
History: The superpowers fought indirectly by backing opposite sides in other conflicts: Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and wars in Africa, including Angola after 1975.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c5.text
History: The USSR launched Sputnik (1957) and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space (1961). The USA landed Apollo 11 astronauts on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c6.text
History: Despite being a dictatorship, Portugal was a founding member of NATO in 1949, largely because of the strategic Azores base. Its colonial wars from 1961 strained relations with allies.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c7.text
History: In the 1970s tensions eased with arms control treaties. In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), loosened Soviet control.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c8.text
History: On 9 November 1989 the Berlin Wall opened. Communist governments across eastern Europe collapsed within months, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

P.title: hi-coldwar.c9.text
History: The Cold War shaped borders, alliances, technologies like the internet and GPS (both born from military research), and conflicts that still echo today.

P.title: hi-modern.q0.q
History: When was Nelson Mandela elected president of South Africa?

P.title: hi-modern.q1.q
History: What happened to extreme poverty between 1950 and 2019?

P.title: hi-modern.q1.o1
History: It fell from about half of humanity to under 10%

P.title: hi-modern.q2.q
History: What goal did the 2015 Paris Agreement set?

P.title: hi-modern.c0.text
History: Between 1945 and 1975, most colonies in Asia and Africa became independent: India and Pakistan (1947), Indonesia, Ghana (1957), dozens of African nations around 1960, and the Portuguese colonies in 1974–75.

P.title: hi-modern.c1.text
History: Movements fought discrimination: the US civil rights movement led by Martin Luther King Jr., the end of apartheid in South Africa with Nelson Mandela's election in 1994, and women's rights movements worldwide.

P.title: hi-modern.c2.text
History: From the 1951 coal and steel community, European cooperation grew into the EU: a single market, free movement, and for many members, the euro.

P.title: hi-modern.c3.text
History: After Mao's era, Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 opened China's economy. Hundreds of millions escaped poverty, and China became the world's manufacturing centre.

P.title: hi-modern.c4.text
History: Container shipping, cheaper flights, trade agreements and the internet tied economies together. Goods are made from parts produced in many countries.

P.title: hi-modern.c5.text
History: The share of people in extreme poverty fell from roughly half of humanity in 1950 to under 10% before the pandemic, one of history's great achievements, though progress is uneven.

P.title: hi-modern.c6.text
History: Terrorist attacks on New York and Washington killed nearly 3,000 people and led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq and a global focus on terrorism.

P.title: hi-modern.c7.text
History: The 2008 crash, starting with US housing loans, triggered a global recession and, in Europe, a debt crisis that led to bailouts of Greece, Ireland and Portugal.

P.title: hi-modern.c8.text
History: COVID-19 spread worldwide from early 2020, causing millions of deaths, lockdowns and the fastest vaccine development in history.

P.title: hi-modern.c9.text
History: Since the 1980s scientists have warned of global warming from greenhouse gases. The 2015 Paris Agreement set the goal of limiting warming to well below 2 °C.

P.title: hi-digital.summary
History: From room-sized computers to smartphones and AI.

P.title: hi-digital.q0.q
History: Who invented the World Wide Web?

P.title: hi-digital.q1.q
History: When was Portugal's Multibanco network launched?

P.title: hi-digital.q1.x
History: One of the world's most advanced ATM systems.

P.title: hi-digital.q2.o1
History: An early US research network, forerunner of the internet

P.title: hi-digital.c0.text
History: Wartime code-breaking and calculations drove early electronic computers. ENIAC (1945) filled a room, weighed 27 tonnes and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes.

P.title: hi-digital.c1.text
History: The transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (1958) made computers smaller, cheaper and more reliable. Intel's 4004 (1971) put a whole processor on one chip.

P.title: hi-digital.c2.text
History: In the late 1970s and 1980s, computers entered homes and offices: the Apple II (1977), IBM PC (1981), Macintosh (1984) and Microsoft Windows. In Portugal the ZX Spectrum (Timex) was hugely popular.

P.title: hi-digital.c3.text
History: ARPANET connected US research computers in 1969. TCP/IP (1983) let networks join into one internet. Portugal connected to the internet in the early 1990s through its universities.

P.title: hi-digital.c4.text
History: At CERN in 1989–91, Tim Berners-Lee invented the web: web pages, links and browsers on top of the internet. He gave it away for free.

P.title: hi-digital.c5.text
History: Google (1998) organised the web; Facebook (2004), YouTube (2005) and Twitter (2006) made everyone a publisher, changing news, politics and friendship.

P.title: hi-digital.c6.text
History: Mobile phones spread fast in the 1990s; Portugal had one of Europe's highest adoption rates. The iPhone (2007) and Android turned phones into pocket computers.

P.title: hi-digital.c7.text
History: Portugal's Multibanco network, launched in 1985, was one of the world's most advanced ATM systems, letting people pay bills, top up phones and buy tickets long before this was common elsewhere.

P.title: hi-digital.c8.text
History: Since the 2000s, computing moved into huge data centres. Companies rent servers on demand (AWS 2006, Azure 2010), and data became one of the most valuable resources.

P.title: hi-digital.c9.text
History: Deep learning (2012), the Transformer (2017) and ChatGPT (2022) opened a new chapter: computers that understand and generate language, images and code.
